 * Sign up and specify their blood group.
 * Log in securely.
 * Search for nearby donors by blood type and location.
 * View donor availability and contact them.
 * Post and respond to urgent blood requests.
 * Create detailed blood donation requests.
 * Find nearby blood donation centers.
Essentially, it's a platform designed to streamline the process of finding, requesting, and donating blood to save lives within the community.

Excited to share my latest project: Food Share (a Food Donation Management System ) built using HTML,CSS,Bootstrap,Javascript,Node.js, Express.js, Mongodb and ejs. This project is designed to ease the process of helping those in need. Our platform connects three types of users—admins, donors, and agents—to ensure a smooth and efficient donation process. Admins can accept/reject donations, and select agents. Donors, on the other hand, can easily make donation requests, track their status, and view both current and past donations. Agents are the ones who collect food from donors' homes and ensure it reaches those who need it most.

Github: https://lnkd.in/d3_82M7W
Live Site: https://lnkd.in/dqYFBKK4

Politics (wayyy) aside.

But this has got to be one of the worst openers to a donation request I’ve ever read 🤦‍♀️.

No one is “waiting for the perfect time” to donate to a political campaign.

No one is sitting around, wondering: “Now? is NOW the time? … What about NOW?”

What they ARE waiting for is a good reason to donate AT ALL.

This is an important lesson for fundraising copy, and copy in general.

You might live and breathe your cause, but the people you’re speaking to have busy lives and many demands on their attention.

They need a compelling reason to read the next line of your message.

So imagine how compelling you have to be to get them to enter their credit card info into a donation form.

Your copy is working against a very strong tide called LIFE. Which means it needs to work really, really hard.

So, give them that reason. Make your cause relevant to their lives. Show them how their contribution can make a real difference. Paint a vivid picture of the positive impact their donation will have. Make it urgent—why is their support needed right now?

Another takeaway from this:

Even some presidential campaign “experts” need to learn copywriting 101:

KNOW. YOUR. AUDIENCE.

Do you know what reciprocity and cheese have in common? The answer is…

They both have an expiration date.

For reciprocity, it’s known as reciprocity decay. (For cheese, it’s known as yuck.)

Turns out you can’t give something and expect to have an infinite IOU.

One hospital found this out the hard way.

They sent over 18,000 donation requests to former patients at various times.

The former patients who received a request soon after their care were *most likely* to donate.

But as time passed between patients’ stays and the donation request, the donations began to decline.

And at a specific point in time, donations plummeted *dramatically*—(I’m talking 30%).

Do you think the power of reciprocity declines at

A) 14 days
B) 30 days

Share your guess in the comments, and I’ll reveal the answer.

–

P.S. The lesson for marketers? 

If you’re asking for a review or testimonial, make the request ASAP. The more time that passes, the more reciprocity decays.

text:
Donor relationship – Expectation vs reality

To understand what a customer wants, ask yourself what you would want as a customer. 
To understand what a donor expects, become a donor for 3-4 non-profits and monitor your experience. Consider what feels welcoming and what seems annoying. 

Here are some common gaps between expectations and reality I've observed as both a non-profit professional and a donor.
 
(1)   Transparency
 
Donor's Expectation: Donors want clear information about fund utilization, ground reports, and the organization's vision and strategy.

Reality: Professionals often present an overly optimistic picture, avoiding questions with exaggerated claims.

Solution: Clearly communicate what you are doing and explain the reasons behind it.
 
(2)   Recognition

Expectation: Acknowledge their contribution and make them feel involved in your vision.

Reality: Bombard them with thank-you emails and send numerous fridge magnets.

Solution: Publicly acknowledge their support, with their consent. Ensure that the appreciation is genuine and that you truly value their contribution, not just for show.

(3)   Donor Communication 

Expectation: Donors want timely documents, relevant updates, and a direct contact number for a real person to reach out to. 

Reality: Numerous automated emails, often with donation requests in every message, and an IVR donor support number that is rarely answered.

Solution: Assign a personalized donor account manager for direct contact, segment your donors based on their preferences, and send relevant content at appropriate intervals.
 
(4)   Trust 

Expectation: Donors should be able to develop confidence in the organization's leadership and mission.

Reality: Donors often learn about organizational developments through news articles.

Solution: The top leadership should send personalized emails to donors at least once a year, discussing recent developments, achievements (and maybe shortfalls too), along with the annual report.
 
(5)   Engagement 

Expectation: Donors want to be asked for their input, informed about key decisions, and have opportunities to interact with beneficiaries.

Reality: Too many calls, unorganised e mailers and frequent & aggressive requests for additional donations.

Solution: Share valuable content at balanced intervals, conduct donor visits and feedback surveys, invite them to volunteer, if feasible send video messages from the leader discussing progress - keeping donor at the centre of communication.

This last week I had the opportunity to present to my colleagues at the University of Minnesota Foundation about the Great Wealth Transfer and the impacts it will have on philanthropy (big thanks to Kristi Flanagan Villar and Jonna Schnettler)

In the next decade, an estimated $16T is expected to be passed down from the Baby Boomer generation to their Gen X and Millennial heirs. However, with most of that transfer expected to benefit the top 10% of households in the U.S., this unprecedented transfer of wealth will further perpetuate wealth gaps that already exist in our country.

Historically, white people have been over-represented in the world of philanthropy as a result of the wide racial wealth gap in the U.S. Knowing how the Great Wealth Transfer is expected to perpetuate this gap, I was interested in learning more about what our role as non-profit and philanthropy professionals should be in practicing inclusive and community-centric donor practices as a way to combat the inequities of the wealth transfer. 

The article below are my thoughts on this topic, but I know there is so much more work to be done (and maybe already has been done by others) in order to better understand how non-profits should approach the Great Wealth Transfer.

The art and science of the "ask."

Ever wonder why some donation requests work better than others?

Recent research on PayPal's Giving Fund website uncovered fascinating insights about donor behavior:

1. The power of options: Replacing a less popular $75 button with either $10 or $200 increased overall donations.

2. Lower amounts = more donors: A $10 option encouraged more people to give (though average donation size decreased).

3. Higher amounts = more funds: A $200 option boosted total money raised.

4. Long-term impact: New options increased the likelihood of future donations for up to 18 months!

5. Personalization matters: Tailoring ask amounts based on factors like income or donation history can optimize results.

The key takeaway? There's no one-size-fits-all approach. It's about finding the right balance for your audience. Remember, cookie cutters are for cookies, not a fundraising strategy.

For fundraisers, this means:
• Regularly analyzing popular donation amounts
• Experimenting with different ask strings
• Considering personalized approaches

In your fundraising appeal, the call to action should resound with one clear and compelling directive: Give Now.

Yet, this straightforward message often gets clouded. Here's where the pitfalls lie in many fundraising efforts:

1. "Share our story." Encouraging supporters to spread the word about your cause is important for visibility, but it's not the same as a direct appeal for funds. While you want your message to reach a wider audience, remember that the act of sharing does not inherently result in financial contributions.

2. "Appreciate our cause." Yes, it's great if donors think positively about your cause. However, goodwill alone doesn't translate to donations. Your primary focus should be motivating supporters to act - to give money - rather than just to appreciate.

3. "Understand this vital information." While educating donors about your cause is beneficial, knowledge itself rarely triggers donations. More often than not, the reverse holds true: individuals who actively donate tend to seek out more knowledge about the cause they support.

4. "Change your mind." Challenging and changing pre-existing notions is a complex process. A simple letter or email isn't sufficient to catalyze such a profound shift. Action, especially in the form of giving, often leads to a change in thought.

Sometimes, we commit the sin of asking people to do other things (people will always take the path of least resistance and think they did their part), such as:

5. "Follow us on social media." While increasing your online following can raise awareness and reach, simply gaining followers doesn't assure funding. Don't mistake social media engagement for a financial commitment to your cause.

6. "Volunteer with us." Calling for volunteers is crucial for many nonprofits, but it doesn't lead to direct fundraising. Volunteers provide invaluable time and skills, but these requests can distract from immediate financial needs if not balanced with clear donation requests.

Your call to action should be a compelling invitation: "Give now. Your gift can transform the world in this specific, tangible way."

This message should be clear, unambiguous, and powerful. Don't bury it, don't overshadow it with less critical tasks, and most importantly, don't understate its importance. Ensure your communication amplifies this call to action and illustrates how each donation can make a significant, meaningful impact.

What If philanthrotigue were a word? I was musing on donor fatigue recently, and the concept of philanthrotigue came to mind, combining elements of philanthropy (the desire to promote the welfare of others, often through charitable acts) with fatigue (a state of exhaustion or weariness).
 
ChatGPT suggests that philanthrotigue could describe:

A weariness or burnout caused by continuous efforts to help others – such as a philanthropist feeling overwhelmed by the scale of need or the demands of their charitable work.

Cynicism or frustration about the effectiveness of philanthropy – a sense of disillusionment that the resources or efforts devoted to helping others may not yield meaningful change.

Compassion fatigue in the context of giving or volunteering – a state where someone feels emotionally drained from persistent exposure to causes or requests for help.

Philanthrotigue could also capture the feeling of weariness or frustration people experience from being constantly solicited for donations or charitable contributions – the mental or emotional exhaustion that arises when someone is inundated with requests to give, whether from organizations, social media campaigns, or personal appeals.

So, what does this mean for us as fundraising professionals or volunteers and the nonprofit organizations we serve?  Make every ask Strategic, Intentional, Targeted, and Well-timed.

At the risk of being a woman who returns to work and struggles to talk about anything but being a mother…

This world mental health day I want to say I’ve found that return harder than I expected. Knowing who I am, and accepting the fact I can never give both jobs 100%. Every parent knows this but it’s a harsh reality facing it when you have to leave a client dinner early, or look after a sick child at home in the week.

I’ve found myself gravitating towards this concept of matrescence (look it up, ask yourself why it’s not mainstream) and how life-changing the peri-natal period (and tbh, for years afterwards) is. I’m re-learning everything about myself, and can’t expect to be the same ‘work self’ I was before either.

I’m leaning on some really supportive colleagues and mentors. I’m using a pretty cool app (Smiling Mind) my mum showed me - she’s brilliantly in-touch with her mental health for a boomer. And I’m trying to lead with kindness knowing that if I’m going through a lot behind the smiling face on video calls, other people are too.

One of the lessons I’m learning is OUTWARD thinking, seeing people as people with their own complex, caring, grappling minds. If you can seek to understand where your colleagues might be coming from rather than how you’d react to the situation, and empathise with that difference, you can turn an interaction or potential conflict on its head. After all our difference is our strength!

Life as a working mum is in actual fact pretty good right now. But it’s okay to find it tough too. I'm here as a listening ear for anyone who may need to talk. 🧠 💛 💬

One of our core values at The Realest Recruiter - Recruitment Company is 

Transparency.

So here is the breakdown of our recruiting process.

1. Meet with the hiring manager and run a full intake call. 

We want to understand why the position is open, why there are no internal candidates, how long the position has been open, how many other agencies they've worked with, how many candidates they’ve interviewed, salary requirements, what success looks like in the role… etc.

2. Calibration sourcing: We present 10-15 profiles for review to calibrate. This is also the opportunity to test the water to see if there are similar industries or skill sets we could tap into. We also agree on the marketing and messaging we will use to reach out to targets and our screening scripts. (this saves a lot of time, and eliminates redundant questions)

3. Initial sourcing: We source and begin to line up conversations with candidates. All conversations are recorded using Metaview and then summarized for the client to view.

4. Biweekly reporting. We share all our activity and provide analytics on the market. Including salary information, brand favorability, and general interest in the role.

5. Speed and quality: Within 5 days of sourcing candidates are presented in real-time.

6. We will communicate, and coordinate the scheduling of interviews, and conduct debrief calls after each step of the interview to make sure parties are aligned on salary, role, and mutual interest.

7. We will repeat until an offer is made and then work with both parties to close the search and avoid declines and counteroffers.

8. Provide checkups through onboarding to make sure the candidate shows up and both parties are happy. Then check-ins for 30 and 60 days.

Each candidate is different,
And each client is different so the process can vary.

But it’s anything but just posting and praying.

What’s your process?

I could recall when I worked as a Vendor support in an online marketplace and it was mandatory to send out daily activity reports at the end of each day. 

Since then, it has been instilled in me to always make a report on anything I do for a client.
resharedPost/text:
Everybody thinks Recruiters don't do anything, but that's not true.

It's not that we don't do anything.

It's that sometimes we don't do a great job telling the people that should know what we're doing.

𝐅𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐫 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭?

It's a report I send to all my hiring managers every Friday to keep them up to date on the job search.

Nothing too crazy, it's simply a snapshot of my quantitative numbers with a narrative written under it for context on what I've done that week.

When most clients receive it there's always a little EXTRA smile on their thank you reply email…

I'd say 90% of my clients say they've never received an activity report from their Recruiter, and the other 10% say not THIS extensive.

The extensive comes from me putting my thoughts into WHY and HOW I did what I did.

Where I'm sourcing... Why I'm sourcing there.

Many clients have NO IDEA what I do when I'm looking for people for their job and sometimes when I present candidates they wonder why this one and not that one.

So I tell them.

And I keep a paper trail.

I love ALLLLLL my partners, but I've had a partner or two come back to me 4...5...6 weeks later ...

"You didn't do anything"...

and then I send them 5 weeks of activity reports they signed off on and...

🦗

It's not a gotcha. It's a protecting the time and energy you've put into a process and being the guide showing the other side how you got to that end result.

My math teacher Mr. Grabowski always loved when I showed my work.

He'd be proud.

Involving 61 companies and around 2,900 workers, this is the world’s largest four-day week trial to date. 
 
 Quick facts:

🤸‍♂️ 92% of the participating employers are sticking with the four-day week
 
 🤸‍♂️ Company revenue rose by 1.4% on average
 
 🤸‍♂️ 96% of workers prefer the four-day week
 
 🤸‍♂️ Employee stress levels dropped by 39%

 🤸‍♂️ 54% of workers felt a reduction in negative emotions
 
 🤸‍♂️60% of employees with care responsibilities saw an improvement to their work-life balance, and 62% reported a positive impact to their social lives
 
 🤸‍♂️ 48% of employees feel more satisfied than when they first started
 
 🤸‍♂️ Sick days plummeted by 65%
 
 🤸‍♂️ Staff resignations dropped by 57%

A Headhunter on LinkedIn reached out to me.
He was looking to place a CEO for a candy company.
Very niche.
Very lucrative.

I pulled recent clients, and sent him a resume for a guy (with his permission) who was a CEO for a wine and spirits company.

Great guy. Super successful. Took this wine company from the brink of bankruptcy to not only being profitable, but growing, with a great culture and long-term plans. Before he got there, it was pretty awful.

So, the headhunter responds back that this is not their guy. The company wants someone with candy experience.

Now, I get absolutely nothing out of this deal, (other than helping a client out), but this response pisses me off.

So I say, "what the hell is the difference if it's wine or candy, leadership is about people/culture/growth, not products. YOU reached out to me. Take 15 minutes and talk to the guy."

He agrees. Long story short, my client just signed an employment agreement to be their new CEO.

It doesn't really matter if your company sells candy or fuselages or shoes, leadership is universal.

Hiring needs to STOP making up rules as they go along.

I interviewed a candidate through Skype last week.

During the call, I heard kids crying in the background. His wife was also talking. The experience was too noisy.

The room he sat was clumsy. I was a bit disappointed.
I expected a more professional approach from him.

Somehow, he felt my disappointment while answering my questions and became unsettled. He stuttered several times.

After the interview, I told him I wasn't impressed with how he presented himself.
He burst into tears, "I am sorry, Sir. I live in a room with my family. There's nowhere they could have stayed.

"We used to live in a bigger apartment before I lost my job three years ago. This is all I can afford for now. I have failed my family. I know I have." He said in tears.

I felt bad. I had no idea that he was going through a tough time.
I apologized and encouraged him not to feel heartbroken. After all, he's trying his best.

Besides, he did well in the interview.
I gave him the contract and asked if he'd like to start next month.

He couldn't believe it because he thought I was going to dismiss him.

He shouted out for joy, "Hey baby, I got the job."
I saw his wife came to hug him.
I was moved.

I learned never to judge anyone. Life isn't balanced. Let's try to make someone smile.

#behuman

¿NOS PERMITIMOS SENTIR LAS EMOCIONES CUANDO SE PRESENTAN EN NUESTRA VIDA?

«Una emoción no causa dolor. La resistencia o supresión de una emoción causa dolor».
— Frederick Dodson.

Cuántas veces no nos hemos recriminado el expresar un sentimiento, por ejemplo, el estar tristes o llorar, pues eso nos han dicho desde que estamos pequeños, que no lloremos porque es signo de debilidad. 🤔

Es normal sentir emociones, pues cuando se presentan, algo nos quieren decir, entonces sintámoslas y vivámoslas, pues de esa forma aprenderemos más sobre nosotros y sobre la situación que está desencadenando dicha emoción. 😕

Escuchando un podcast días atrás, en él mencionaban que cuando alguien tiene un mal día, hace todo lo posible por estar bien, por sentirse alegre, pero las circunstancias en esos momentos no están para expresar ese estado de ánimo, entonces, comentaban en el programa, “dejemos que el tigre nos abrace”, siendo que el tigre puede ser el miedo, la tristeza, el enojo o cualquier otra emoción no tan grata, pero que algo nos viene a mostrar. 😕

A partir de que validemos nuestro sentir, es que podremos accionar para seguir adelante, obtener la lección que tengamos que aprender y continuar con nuestra vida, saliendo de ese episodio mucho más fortalecidos y sabiendo que no todo dura para siempre y que, volverán a haber días como esos en los que no estamos bien, pero también habrá días que disfrutemos. 😎

Valoremos nuestras emociones, dándoles cabida en nuestra vida y entendiendo el porqué es que se presentan. 👍

Este método consiste en dividir el tiempo en bloques de trabajo de 25 minutos, en donde te enfocas en una tarea específica y se trabaja sin distracciones ni interrupciones. Después de cada pomodoro, se toma un descanso de 5 minutos para descansar y recargar energías antes de comenzar el siguiente bloque.

En lo particular me sirve más con bloques de 50 min y descansas 10 min.

Great managers create stability for their teams, even when things within the larger organization feel up in the air. 

If you're a manager, here are a few ways to do exactly that:

1. Make emotional proofreads a habit. Don't send an email that just says, "Let's talk," when you mean, "The draft you sent was great. Let's find time to chat through next steps." 

2. Set clear goals and celebrate mini-milestones. People tend to feel more secure (and are more likely to take the breaks they need) if they know they're moving forward on the right things.

3. Acknowledge what people are feeling. Even just saying something like, “I know a lot is changing, and that can be stressful. Let me know what I can do to support you,” can go a long way.

What actions do you think differentiate great managers from good managers?

La estrategia de Kaizen es el concepto de mayor importancia en la administración japonesa. Ya desde 1986 Masaaki Imai fundó el Kaizen Institute, centro dedicado al trabajo de consultorio para implementas la “mejora continua” y progresiva que involucre a todos, desde la alta administración, gerentes y trabajadores. Esta filosofía es aplicable en cualquier trabajo y muchas de sus prácticas pueden aplicarse para lograr una ventaja competitiva considerable.La esencia de Kaizen supone que nuestra forma de vida sea nuestra vida de trabajo, vida social o vida familiar, la cual merece ser mejorada de manera constante. Cabe destacar que la estrategia será eficaz si se trata de hacer mejoras que estén conectadas a resultados medibles y a un objetivo más profundo. Un ejemplo en la mejora de procesos es el Children’s Medical Center de Dallas, Texas, donde simplemente se preguntas “¿existe una forma mejor?”, vinculando la mejora concreta en un departamento para tal propósito y a la misión de la organización preguntando a su equipo si los cambios propuestos ayudarán a conseguir “una mejor atención para los niños”.
El Kaizen es aplicable a cualquier  sistema de organización...

Aprendiendo de los grandes…

El Sábado Coldplay dio un mega concierto en Bogotá, y más allá de la emoción musical y nivel de evento que fue y que representó para miles de Colombianos, me dejó varias lecciones valiosas que muchos de nosotros podemos aplicar en nuestros roles como líderes de empresas.

1) Sé agradecido y empático con tus clientes! Empezaron el concierto agradeciendo y siendo empáticos con la difícil situación que hemos vivido con el Covid y con la coyuntura actual del país! 

2) Sé humilde y busca llegar a todos tus clientes con las mejores propuesta, no sólo enfocarse en quienes pagan más. Buscaron llegar a todo el estadio… la estructura del show estaba diseñada para llegar de cerca a todos y no pararon de intentarlo y comunicarlo toda la noche!

3) No sólo vendas tu producto, sino enfócate en dar experiencias! El show fue mucho más que el alucinante repertorio musical que tienen. Buscaron integrar a todos los presentes con la música, con mensajes de unidad, todos saltando y cantando juntos, luces, fuegos artificiales… alucinante!

4) No importa en el negocio o industria que estés, busca a ese cliente… a esa persona a la que le puedas hacer cumplir un sueño! Le cantó en vivo a una chica frente a todo el estadio e hizo su sueño realidad! 

5) Finalmente, y sin duda dejando muchos más puntos por mencionar, trabaja duro y entrégalo todo por tu trabajo, por tu negocio o por tu pasión! Lo entregaron todo minuto a minuto, no pararon, se esforzaron, bailaron, saltaron!!!!

Realmente más que un gran evento y concierto, una lección de humildad… los grandes como ellos, son grandes porque entendieron la verdadera fórmula del éxito!

resharedPost/text:
5 TIPS PARA MEJORAR COMO SE MUESTRAN HABILIDADES EN UN CV
 
 LA INFORMACIÓN VS. LO ESTRATÉGICO
 
 Para que los candidatos puedan mostrar bien las habilidades en un Cv es necesario tener en cuenta lo siguiente:
 

 1. Describir tu toma de decisiones 
 
Es necesario clasificar, analizar y priorizar las tareas en cada puesto función de su toma de decisiones
Cuando se tiene que presentar un Cv es importante que se ponga foco en cómo tomabas decisiones y cuales son aquellas funciones del cargo que precisaban esa acción inmediata. Por ejemplo, una tarea estándar como asignar turnos es importante por lo que representa y por el significado de sus consecuencias a nivel global,
 
 2. Dar importancia al Trabajo en equipo
 
Antes de fijar la versión final del texto fíjate si en el se habla de los logros de los equipos que lideraste o de los cuales participaste es fundamental conocer cuál es la capacidad productiva de cada persona y dejar siempre un pequeño margen a la interacción con el equipo
Hay que tener cuidado con las palabras que se emplean para que no se diluyan tus logros y responsabilidades dentro de cada proyecto o cargo desarrollado, pues pueden suponer que tu liderazgo quede claro o a presentar un proyecto 
 
 3. Enfocarte en la consistencia de los resultados
 
Cuando se redacta un Cv, es crucial asignar un espacio a mostrar resultados de cada puesto descrito Aunque pueden surgir ciertas situaciones especiales, lo normal es que además de señalar la ejecución de una tarea se muestre los en la posición descrita
Si muestras una carrera debe quedar claro cuál ha sido tu avance en los logros de metas y cuan bueno eres superándote al cambiar de oportunidad
 
 4. Trabajar tu capacidad de Comunicación 
 
Si una persona trabaja en armar un CV debe tener un estilo claro y directo, que tienda a lograr el objetivo de llamar la atención de manera positiva. Por eso, es necesario controlar muy bien lo que escribes, y lo que no escribes aunque pueda resultar contradictorio al pasar a la siguiente etapa que es la entrevista
 Si no se redacta adecuadamente y se prioriza no se puede saber de toda tu experiencia que es lo INDISPENSABLE que esté presente También hay que considerar la buena ortografía, las frases correctas, y no poner el Cv en spanglish. Para esto es necesario, una vez más, diferenciar lo importante de lo indispensable y tener una buena planificación del contenido
 
 5. Mostrar tu Nivel Real de tu experiencia
 
Hay que tener claro cuál es el cometido a realizar y darle prioridad a la experiencia: que encaje con lo que la empresa necesita en el nivel de responsabilidad que necesita, algunas veces los puestos se pueden nombrar igual pero no requieren las mismas experiencias
 
En definitiva, si los contenidos que tiene un CV son adecuados y se manejan con efectividad todas los puntos acá mencionados, se tendrá una mayor satisfacción y logros de entrevistas para disfrutar con la familia o los amigos con un nuevo empleo

CUANDO SER FELIZ EN EL TRABAJO NO SIGNIFICA ESTAR SIEMPRE CONTENTO Y SONRIENDO TODO EL TIEMPO. De la utopía a la realidad. 

En un trabajo habrán días más complicados que otros, habrán desafíos duros. Las cosas no siempre saldrán como lo planeado, habrán reclamos que atender, gente difícil, injusticias.

Habrán días en los que no dan ganas de ir a trabajar, en los que se cuentan los minutos deseando que se termine el turno para salir.

A veces suele ser duro, no es un cuento de hadas. Lo sabemos.

Pero por lo general, es un lugar donde podemos cubrir nuestro propósito, desafiarnos, crecer, desarrollarnos, aprender.

Es un lugar donde podemos encontrar las oportunidades de fluir y sentirnos bien por superar los problemas y desafíos con nuestros talentos, por ayudar a otros y que nuestras habilidades sean valoradas por ello.

Hay problemas, si, pero están ahí para ser solucionados y cuando los superamos, nos sentimos orgullosos, con satisfacción. El goce maravilloso de sentir que cumplimos con la tarea.

Sentirnos útiles y sorprendidos de nuestras capacidades y crecimiento.

Eso es un lugar donde podemos sentirnos felices, nuestro lugar, nuestro trabajo.

Sé lo que te cuesta, sé lo que lo valoras.

Cuéntame como lo sientes tú, cuéntame tu orgullo.

Ariel Hernández

CULTURAS DE TRABAJO TÓXICAS - UN CÍRCULO VICIOSO DAÑINO. Cuanto más tiempo te quedes dentro, peor estarás y menos posibilidades de salir tendrás.

Estar dentro de un círculo vicioso implica hacer una y otra vez un mismo acto, repetir una escena, una situación, obteniendo los mismos resultados o similares.

Nuestra mente tiende a la repetición, a volver a lo conocido, a lo que nos da comodidad, a repetir conductas que aunque nos hagan daño las volvemos a poner en práctica.

Es importante conocernos y observarnos para saber qué es lo que nos está haciendo mal y producir cambios saludables para alejarnos de esa zona que nos genera sufrimiento.

Esto provoca la sensación de falta de salida, ausencia de alternativas, incapacidad de elegir otra cosa diferente. Estar en un círculo vicioso es sentirse en un callejón sin salida.

Nos quejamos, sufrimos, nos molestamos, sin darnos cuenta de que para salir de esa repetición perjudicial tenemos que tomar decisiones que nos permitan romper con ese círculo que nos genera desgaste y sufrimiento.

TU SALUD MENTAL Y EMOCIONAL NO SON NEGOCIABLES.

Cuanto antes lo detectes actúa para encontrar la mejor salida, o pide ayuda.

El mejor trabajador es despedido:
El mejor jugador de fútbol del mundo sintió la frustración y dolor y no tuvo una buena experiencia en la desvinculación.

“Me hubiera gustado irme de otra manera”, frase de Messi que todos alguna vez experimentamos.

Sentir que dejamos todo en ese trabajo y que no fuimos valorados, que los sacrificios no fueron percibidos.

Estar desempleado es momentáneo, no te define ni como persona ni como profesional. Estar desempleado es una oportunidad de cerrar una etapa y empezar una nueva. Estar desempleado es una invitación a recobrar la confianza en uno mismo y recuperar la motivación y energía de ir Pa Lante.

Lecciones para los que gestionamos personas:
📌 Siempre dar espacio para que se expresen (speak up): entrevista de salida.
📌 Velar por el equilibrio en el trabajo y vida personal.
📌 Cuida y paga bien a los que generan resultados, nadie hará el trabajo mejor que ellos. Se paga por resultados, no por trabajar.
📌 El talento senior vale más que el potencial sin realizar, porque son ejemplos de éxito y atraen más talento.
📌 Siempre ten un plan de sucesión.
📌 No hagas que los malos echen a los buenos (Ley de Gresham en el Talento).

Verbos de acción para tu HV o CV. 

Quizas uno de los dilemas que más se presentan al redactar tu nuevo CV o actualizar tu perfil en #LinkedIn es ¿Cómo inicio? ¿Cómo redacto?. Bueno aquí te dejo unos de los verbos en acción más aplicable para orientar tu perfil a resultados debido a tu experiencia. 

▫️Verbos para expresar tu desarrollo dentro de la empresa: desarrollar, expandir, incrementar, organizar, aumentar, conseguir, promover, resolver.
▫️ Verbos para indicar habilidades ejecutivas y directivas: liderar, supervisar, fundar, guiar, gestionar, dirigir, aprobar.
▫️ Verbos para indicar habilidades financieras: administrar, pronosticar, presupuestar, elaborar, calcular, registrar.
▫️Verbos para clasificar habilidades creativas: diseñar, componer, crear, personalizar.

Otro punto importante es que antes de que redactes tu CV tengas un poco claro esto:

Muchas de las personas que están aquí pasan por un momento diferente a lo que han vivido antes. Tras el despido o el NO en un proceso de selección, las personas necesitan superar este periodo. Este conlleva la adaptación emocional a lo que acaba de ocurrir.

 Muchas personas afectadas reaccionan sumiéndose en un estado de pasividad. Otras pueden llegar a enviar muchos  currículums antes de aceptar esta situación. El duelo justamente tiene que ver con eso con la 'adaptación emocional' que surge ante esto.

Sheneider (1984) “el duelo es también un proceso que afecta a la totalidad de la persona a nivel físico, emocional y espiritual.”

Dershimer (1990) “el duelo es más que el sufrimiento emocional y el dolor, es un proceso que incluye cambios significativos en las actitudes, valores, pensamientos y creencias de quien lo experimenta.”

Este proceso nos lleva a encontrarnos con nosotros y a levantarnos con nuevos aprendizajes donde nosotros mismo experimentamos y que nadie nos ha contado. 

En la imagen detallo las 5 fases del duelo de la Psiquiatra Elisabeth Kübler-Ross.

How The Iron Dome Identifies Missiles That Need to Be Intercepted

If you've ever wondered how air defense systems know exactly which threat is about to appear and where, it's all thanks to radar.

Radar is a system that detects objects by emitting radio waves. These waves are sent into the air and spread out in all directions. The moment they hit an object, they immediately bounce back to the system.

The radar receives the reflected waves and, through data processing of the returning wave, calculates the distance, location, and speed of the object that needs to be intercepted.

By the way, in the picture, you can see an MMR radar produced by the ELTA Systems Ltd Division.
It is used in both the Iron Dome and David's Sling, both of which were developed under the leadership of the Israel Missile Defense Organization at the DDR&D, with Rafael Advanced Defense Systems as the main developer.
